questions.title: Is the deprivation of valuable economic information a protected property interest under §1348?
questions.question_body: In *United States v. Constantinescu*, the district court dismissed the indictment because it allegedly failed to allege that defendants deprived victims of a protected property interest. The indictment, however, alleges that defendants “intended to deprive followers of potentially valuable economic information” while also stating that they induced followers to purchase securities. This sounds similar to *Ciminelli v. United States*, where the Supreme Court said a right to valuable economic information was not a protected property interest. I’m confused about how the presence of the *fraudulent‑inducement* element changes the analysis. Does the fact that followers were induced to part with money make the deprivation of money a property interest protected by §1348, and if so, why does that satisfy the statutory requirement?

questions.title: What is the difference between the Supreme Court’s ‘right‑to‑control’ theory and the ‘fraudulent‑inducement’ theory in securities fraud?
questions.question_body: The opinion compares *Ciminelli*’s right‑to‑control theory with the fraudulent‑inducement theory invoked in *Kousisis*. I’m struggling to understand how the courts distinguish these two concepts and why the indictment in *Constantinescu* is analyzed under the latter instead of the former. Specifically, how does the fraudulent‑inducement theory protect the victim’s money or property, whereas the right‑to‑control theory does not? And why does the court consider the indictment free of the right‑to‑control theory when the alleged fraud is only that followers were misled?

questions.title: What statutory elements must an indictment allege to establish a ‘scheme to defraud’ under 18 U.S.C. §1348?
questions.question_body: The court explains that §1348 requires a scheme to defraud and intent to defraud, referencing cases such as *Evans* and *Kousisis*. I’m unclear about the exact elements the indictment must include to satisfy the scheme element. Does it need to allege a material misrepresentation, a deception, an intent to obtain money or property, and the declaration that such deception was intended to deceive others? Additionally, how much factual detail is required versus what can be inferred from the indictment’s allegations?

questions.title: Does a fraud indictment need to allege that victims suffer real economic loss?
questions.question_body: In *Kousisis*, the Supreme Court held that the ‘fraudulent‑inducement’ theory does not require the victim to suffer a net loss; the defendant only needs to have intended to obtain money or property. In *Constantinescu*, the indictment claims defendants were simply ‘deprived followers of potentially valuable economic information’ yet also ‘induced followers to purchase securities’, which would mean the followers gave up money. I’m confused about whether the indictment must state that the followers actually lost money or that they simply were induced to part with money. Does the lack of a so‑called ‘mirror‑image’ requirement mean the indictment is still sufficient even if followers received equal or greater value in the securities purchased?

questions.title: What standard does the Fifth Circuit apply when reviewing an indictment’s sufficiency, and why can a district court dismiss an indictment that allegedly states a crime?
questions.question_body: The opinion notes that a court reviews sufficiency de novo, with a standard from *Rafoi*, *Fontenot*, *Gaytan*, etc. It lists three requirements: enumerate elements, fairly inform the defendant, and provide a double‑jeopardy defense. I’m confused about how this standard operates in practice. In particular, why did the district court dismiss the *Constantinescu* indictment based on property‑interest issues at all? Is insufficient detail an actual failure of the indictment, or can a court say ‘the indictment fails to state a crime’ because it does not provide all required material elements? Also, how does the de novo review differ from a petition for a more trivial issue?

questions.title: How did the Supreme Court’s decisions in *Ciminelli* and *Kousisis* shape the analysis of sufficiency in *Constantinescu*?
questions.question_body: The Fifth Circuit relies heavily on *Ciminelli* to reject the right‑to‑control theory but refers to *Kousisis* to support the notion that obtaining money without a victim’s net loss is still fraud. I’m struggling to see how the court reconciles the two decisions in this new context. Does *Kousisis* effectively override the property‑interest concern in *Ciminelli*? How does the court apply *Ciminelli* to the allegations that defendants sought to deprive followers of valuable information, yet also alleges wrongful inducement that resulted in the victims paying money?

questions.title: Is it necessary for an indictment to explicitly assure a double‑jeopardy defense to be considered sufficient?
questions.question_body: The sufficiency standard lists (1) enumerating elements, (2) fairly informing the defendant, and (3) providing a double‑jeopardy defense. The *Constantinescu* opinion does not explicitly mention the double‑jeopardy requirement, yet the court focuses on the scheme and intent elements. I’m unsure whether the indictment can be considered sufficient if it does not explicitly mention that it provides a double‑jeopardy defense. Does the mere fact that the indictment is charged with fraud automatically satisfy that requirement, or must it actively include language that explains the defenses a defendant could raise under double jeopardy?
